media.title: Nowiny Codzienne, April 1933 — Kiepura’s Ein Lied für Dich in Berlin
media.description: “Wielkość talentu Jana Kiepury podbija nawet Berlin i Niemcy,” a report from Berlin in Nowiny Codzienne, 1933, no. 81 (April 1933), on the world premiere of Ein Lied für Dich at the Gloria-Palast on Holy Saturday. The paper states that German censorship struck the name of the composer, “p. Bronisław Kaper,” a Pole from Warsaw, from the German version of the film, together with the names of the foreign production managers.
media.altText: Polish newspaper page headed “Wielkość talentu Jana Kiepury podbija nawet Berlin i Niemcy,” with a report on the Berlin premiere of Ein Lied für Dich.

timelineEvents.title: Kaper’s name in German film credits
timelineEvents.label: 1933 · Kaper’s name in German film credits
timelineEvents.shortDescription: In 1933 Kaper’s name was struck from some German film credits and kept in others.
timelineEvents.longDescription: In April 1933 the Polish daily Nowiny Codzienne reported from Berlin that German censorship had removed the name of “p. Bronisław Kaper,” a Pole from Warsaw, from the German version of Ein Lied für Dich, which had just had its premiere at the Gloria-Palast; no other source confirms this. When Ufa released Kind, ich freu’ mich auf Dein Kommen in June, neither Kaper nor Jurmann was named in the credits or the advertising, which gave the music to Hans O. Borgmann. The pattern was not uniform, however. In January 1933 the Berlin censors had banned the poster for Madame wünscht keine Kinder, judging it, together with the film’s title, liable to overexcite young viewers; the decision did not concern the music. Shown as Madame wird kinderlieb, the film was advertised in Bielefeld on 25 August 1933 with the credit “Musik von Jurmann und Kaper,” on the same page as an advertisement for Hans F. K. Günther’s Kleine Rassenkunde des deutschen Volkes, and a Stuttgart cinema notice of September 1934 still named Jurmann and Kaper as its composers.
